source.title: Remote Sensing Semantic Segregation for Water Information Extraction: Optimization of Samples via Training Error Performance
source.authors: Rui Wang; Yizhuo Meng; Wen Zhang; Ziyao Li; Fengmin Hu; Lingkui Meng

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares training behavior on screened and corrupted water-label datasets, including an experiment with 10% corrupted labels. It does not reproduce random relabeling of the full training set.
record.gate_note: The paper's statement that deep networks fit random labels cites Zhang et al. [34]; that cited result is not this paper's evidence. Figure 2 reports training-error curves for three models across three datasets. Figure 4 compares LEV distributions for FCN training on accurate labels and labels with 10% corrupted information.
record.test_reason: The FCN experiment with 10% corrupted labels bears on V6 in remote-sensing segmentation: loss trajectories differ between batches containing corrupted labels and batches without them, and the authors report better learning of correct water information after 20,000 iterations. It does not test V4's corruption-fraction trend or perfect training fit.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that LEV-based sample analysis and filtering improve prediction accuracy and training stability while reducing, but not eliminating, corrupted information. Intervention timing and the number of filtering rounds require manual settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses remote-sensing water segmentation with naturally and deliberately corrupted labels, comparing FCN, Unet and deeplabv3+ training behavior; it does not use the original random-labeling experiment or its measurement setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that network structure does not remove the effect of corrupted information; its corruption comparisons use different label-error types and a 10% replacement condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Across FCN, Unet, and deeplabv3+, systematic annotation errors impair convergence and produce corresponding segmentation mistakes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structured annotation errors can impair convergence and prediction quality across several water-segmentation architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing samples identified by the LEV method improves training stability and prediction accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LEV-based sample filtering can improve water-segmentation training in the reported setting.

record.problems: The training-error and LEV curves are reported in figures without numeric values in the text. The corrupted-label experiment does not test fully random labels or a range of corruption fractions. The paper describes an accurate test set but provides no numeric test-error values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the paper's proposed sample-removal optimization results: those evaluate its data-cleaning method rather than one of the claim versions. Figure-only prediction-accuracy comparisons in Figures 19–21 also do not report numeric values and concern the proposed optimization.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged training settings.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence across increasing corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across random-corruption fractions from none to all.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and their removal.
Eventual memorization of corrupted labels is predicted rather than demonstrated by continued training; fully random-label datasets are not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The original random-label fitting result is cited prior work. Figure graphics are unavailable in the supplied text, so numerical losses and final fit cannot be checked. The record's V4 limits_scope verdict mistakes untested components for negative evidence. The authors describe simultaneous learning at different rates; their later acceleration and eventual equal fidelity for corrupted information are explanatory predictions.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not assign completely random labels to the full training set or report zero or near-zero training error and chance test error under that condition.
It does not measure training time to fit random versus true labels or vary the fraction of corrupted labels to assess a slowdown.
It does not train on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.

It examines a 10% corrupted-label condition and describes training-error behavior, but does not test a range from no corruption to complete corruption, establish perfect training fit throughout, or report test error rising steadily toward chance.
It does not test weight decay, dropout or data augmentation.
It does not compare learning patterns for real and random labels over training; its 10% corrupted-label experiment concerns water and non-water labels.

rows.subject: FCN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a comparison set with 10% of image water labels replaced with non-water labels; LEV-point distribution recorded over 20,000 training times.

conditions.value: 10% of image water labels replaced with non-water labels

rows.note: The authors state that after 20,000 training times the model's expression of water information is better than its expression of error information, and warn that continued training may increase fidelity to both.
rows.check: Relink to V6. The text reports better expression of correct water information than corrupted information after 20,000 iterations. LEV averages distinguish minibatches containing corrupted labels from those without them; they are not separately measured per-pixel accuracies. Replace the figure-only value with this qualitative result.
